subject: DI01000031

intro_text.en: Unit 2 of Communication Skills in English: the eight parts of speech, the eight tense forms the syllabus lists (four present, three past, future simple), the eleven modal auxiliaries, subject-verb agreement and the four basic sentence patterns SV, SVO, SVA and SVC. Grammar is taught by example: one rule line, a table of forms, model sentences and the mistake to avoid. Fifteen answered practice questions are in section 6.

body.en:
Rule

A noun names a person, place, thing or idea.

Five kinds, with examples

KindWhat it namesExamples
Properone particular name, always with a capitalSurat, Gujarat, Ashok, TATA, Monday
Commonany one of a classengineer, motor, workshop, city
Collectivea group as one unitteam, crowd, batch, fleet
Materialwhat a thing is made ofsteel, brass, rubber, cement
Abstracta quality, state or ideahonesty, safety, patience, speed

Countable and uncountable

  • Countable: one bolt, two bolts, three bolts.
  • Uncountable: water, oil, information, advice, equipment, furniture - no plural, no a.

Examples in sentences

Same noun doing different work

  • The motor is hot. (subject)
  • We replaced the motor. (object)
  • The motor casing cracked. (modifier)
  • Ashok works in the tool room at TATA Motors.

Common mistake

"Informations", "advices", "equipments" and "furnitures" do not exist. Say "a piece of information", "two pieces of equipment".

Rule

A verb shows an action (run, weld, check) or a state (be, seem, have, know).

Kinds of verb

KindWorkExamples
Main / lexicalcarries the meaningweld, replace, measure, fail
Auxiliaryhelps the main verbis, are, was, has, have, do, will, can
Transitiveneeds an objectreplace the belt, check the oil
Intransitiveno object neededrun, arrive, sleep, rise
Regularpast in -edcheck → checked, test → tested
Irregularpast changes formwrite → wrote → written, run → ran → run

Examples

Auxiliary + main verb

  • The pump is running.
  • We have replaced the seal.
  • The belt was slipping.
  • He can weld aluminium.

Common mistake

Dropping the auxiliary: "He going to the site" is wrong; write "He is going to the site".

Rule

A pronoun stands in place of a noun so that the noun is not repeated.

Kinds, with examples

KindExamples
Personal (subject / object)I / me, we / us, he / him, they / them
Possessivemy, our, his, their, mine, ours
Reflexivemyself, ourselves, himself, themselves
Demonstrativethis, that, these, those
Relativewho, whom, which, that, whose
Interrogativewho? what? which? whose?
Indefinitesomeone, anything, everybody, none

Examples

In sentences

  • She checked the panel and I recorded the reading.
  • The bearing that failed was new.
  • This is the drawing; those are the spares.
  • The fitter repaired it himself.

Common mistake

"Myself Raj" and "Please contact to myself" are wrong. Write "I am Raj" and "Please contact me".

Rule

An adjective describes or limits a noun: a hot motor, three bolts, brass washers.

Kinds

KindExamples
Qualityhot, long, careful, worn
Quantitysome, enough, little, plenty of
Numberthree, tenth, several
Demonstrativethis panel, those wires
Possessivemy tools, their workshop

Degrees of comparison

PositiveComparativeSuperlative
longlongerlongest
heavyheavierheaviest
goodbetterbest
badworseworst
carefulmore carefulmost careful

Order before a noun

opinion - size - age - colour - origin - material - noun: a useful small old grey Indian steel box.

Examples

Comparison in use

  • This belt is longer than that one.
  • Line 2 is the busiest line in the plant.
  • Today's reading is better than yesterday's.
  • Use the most careful method for the bearing.

Common mistake

"More better", "most best" and "more easier" double the comparison. Use one form only.

Rule

An adverb describes a verb, an adjective or another adverb: runs smoothly, very hot, quite slowly.

Kinds

KindQuestion it answersExamples
Mannerhow?quickly, carefully, badly, well
Timewhen?now, yesterday, soon, already
Placewhere?here, outside, everywhere
Frequencyhow often?always, often, rarely, never
Degreehow much?very, too, almost, enough

How they are formed

  • adjective + -ly: quick → quickly, careful → carefully.
  • irregular: good → well, fast → fast, hard → hard, late → late.
  • Some words are both: a fast motor (adjective), the motor runs fast (adverb).

Examples

Position

  • The pump runs smoothly. (after the verb)
  • He carefully measured the bore. (before the verb)
  • The line stops twice daily. (frequency at the end)
  • The motor is very hot. (degree before an adjective)

Common mistake

"He works good" is wrong because good is an adjective; write "He works well".

Rule

A preposition links a noun or pronoun to another word and shows place, time, direction or agent: under the bench, at 9 am, by the fitter.

Place and time

PrepositionUseExample
ata point, an exact timeat the gate, at 9 am, at night
ona surface, a day or dateon the bench, on Monday, on 5 March
inan enclosed space, a month or yearin the panel, in May, in 2026
under / overbelow / aboveunder the bench, over the pipe
between / amongtwo / more than twobetween the two pumps, among the workers
byagent, or not later thanwelded by Ashok, by Friday
withinstrument or companycut with a hacksaw, with the supervisor
since / forpoint of time / length of timesince Monday, for two hours

Examples

Common pairs

  • The drawing is on the board and the tools are in the box.
  • The job must finish by Friday, and it has been open since Monday.
  • The fault is between the pump and the tank.
  • The report was written by the trainee for the supervisor.

Common mistake

"Discuss about the problem", "married with her", "different than" - write "discuss the problem", "married to her", "different from".

Rule

A conjunction joins words, phrases or clauses: belt and pulley, stop because the guard is loose.

Three kinds

KindWorkExamples
Coordinatingjoins equalsand, but, or, so, for, yet, nor
Subordinatingjoins a dependent clausebecause, although, if, when, while, since, unless, after
Correlativeworks in pairseither ... or, neither ... nor, not only ... but also, both ... and

Examples

In sentences

  • The belt and the pulley were replaced.
  • The line stopped because the coolant ran out.
  • Although the load was high, the motor stayed cool.
  • Either the seal or the gland is leaking.
  • Neither the fitter nor the helper was present.
  • Not only the bearing but also the shaft was damaged.

Common mistake

Using two conjunctions for one link: "Although it was hot, but we finished" is wrong; keep "Although it was hot, we finished".

Rule

An interjection expresses a sudden feeling. It stands apart from the sentence and takes an exclamation mark.

Common interjections

FeelingInterjectionExample
joyhurray!, wow!Hurray! The test passed.
surpriseoh!, what!Oh! The panel is live.
painouch!, ah!Ouch! That edge is sharp.
reliefphew!Phew! The leak has stopped.
sorrowalas!Alas! The batch is scrap.
warninghush!, look out!Look out! The load is slipping.

Register

Interjections belong in speech and informal writing. A technical report says "The batch was rejected", not "Alas! The batch was rejected".

Common mistake

Overusing them in written work. One "oh" in a report looks careless; use a plain statement instead.

Form

TypeStructureExample
Affirmativesubject + V1 (V1+s with he/she/it)The pump runs.
Negativedo / does + not + V1The pump does not run.
Questiondo / does + subject + V1?Does the pump run?

Use

  • Habits and routines: I check the panel every morning.
  • Facts and laws: Water boils at 100 °C.
  • Timetables: The shift starts at 7 am.
  • Instructions: Switch off the mains first.

Examples

Correct forms

  • The fitter checks the oil level daily.
  • The fitters check the oil level daily.
  • The motor does not draw more than 6 A.
  • Do you record the reading in the log book?

Common mistake

"He run the machine" - with he, she or it the verb takes -s: "he runs".

Form

TypeStructureExample
Affirmativeam / is / are + V-ingThe line is running.
Negativeam / is / are + not + V-ingThe line is not running.
Questionam / is / are + subject + V-ing?Is the line running?

Use

  • Happening now: I am checking the bearing.
  • Around now, these days: We are using a new coolant.
  • Fixed near future: We are starting the trial at 4 pm.
  • Complaints with always: He is always losing the spanner.

Examples

Now and around now

  • The compressor is making a noise right now.
  • Two operators are working on the panel.
  • I am not using the crane today.
  • Are you reading the new drawing?

Common mistake

Stative verbs take the simple form: "I am knowing the answer" is wrong; write "I know the answer".

Form

TypeStructureExample
Affirmativehave / has + V3We have replaced the seal.
Negativehave / has + not + V3We have not replaced the seal.
Questionhave / has + subject + V3?Have you replaced the seal?

Use

  • Finished action with a present result: I have finished the job, so the line can start.
  • Experience with no fixed time: He has worked in three plants.
  • With just, already, yet, ever, never, since, for.

Present perfect or past simple?

Present perfectPast simple
no time mentioneda finished time is named
I have checked the panel.I checked the panel at 9 am.
He has worked here for 3 years.He worked here in 2022.

Examples

With markers

  • The job has just finished.
  • I have not received the drawing yet.
  • She has been on this machine since January.
  • Have you ever welded aluminium?

Common mistake

"I have seen him yesterday" is wrong because yesterday is a finished time; write "I saw him yesterday".

Form

TypeStructureExample
Affirmativehave / has been + V-ingHe has been welding for an hour.
Negativehave / has not been + V-ingHe has not been welding.
Questionhave / has + subject + been + V-ing?Has he been welding since 9 am?

Use

An action that started in the past and is still going on now, usually with for (length of time) or since (starting point).

Examples

Still happening

  • The pump has been running for three hours.
  • I have been looking for that spanner since morning.
  • The line has been stopping repeatedly all week.
  • How long have you been working on this panel?

Present perfect or present perfect continuous?

Perfect: resultPerfect continuous: duration
I have painted the guard.I have been painting the guard.
The job is finished.The job is still going on.

Common mistake

Using it for a finished amount: "I have been finishing three jobs" is wrong; write "I have finished three jobs".

Form

TypeStructureExample
Affirmativesubject + V2The belt broke.
Negativedid not + V1The belt did not break.
Questiondid + subject + V1?Did the belt break?

Use

  • A finished action at a finished time: We replaced the belt yesterday.
  • A series of past events: He opened the panel, tested the relay and closed it.
  • Past habits: He worked night shift in 2023.

Markers

yesterday, last week, in 2024, two days ago, then, after that, when.

Examples

Right and wrong

  • The line stopped at 10:15 am.
  • We did not find the cause yesterday.
  • Did you check the coolant before starting?
  • Wrong: "We have replaced it yesterday." Right: "We replaced it yesterday."
  • Wrong: "He did not checked it." Right: "He did not check it."

Common mistake

After did or did not the verb stays in V1 - no -ed, no V2.

Form

TypeStructureExample
Affirmativewas / were + V-ingThe pump was running.
Negativewas / were + not + V-ingThe pump was not running.
Questionwas / were + subject + V-ing?Was the pump running?

Use

  • An action in progress at a past moment: At 10 am we were testing the motor.
  • A longer action interrupted by a shorter one: I was checking the panel when the light went off.
  • Two actions going on together: While he was welding, I was grinding.

Examples

With when and while

  • The operator was cleaning the guard when the alarm rang.
  • While we were waiting, the supervisor called.
  • They were not working after 6 pm.
  • Were you testing the relay at that time?

Common mistake

Using it for a completed single action: "I was replaced the belt" is wrong; write "I replaced the belt".

Form

TypeStructureExample
Affirmativehad + V3The belt had broken.
Negativehad not + V3The belt had not broken.
Questionhad + subject + V3?Had the belt broken?

Use

The earlier of two past actions: both happened in the past, and one happened first.

Examples

Which came first?

  • The line was already down when I reached - the belt had broken before 7 am.
  • We had already replaced the seal before the inspector arrived.
  • He had not checked the torque, so the joint leaked.
  • Had you read the manual before you opened the panel?

Order words

before, after, by the time, already, when - these make the order clear: After we had tested the pump, we started the line.

Common mistake

Using the past perfect for a single past action: "I had gone to the site yesterday" is unnecessary; write "I went to the site yesterday".

Form

TypeStructureExample
Affirmativewill + V1The vendor will deliver on Monday.
Negativewill not (won't) + V1The vendor will not deliver today.
Questionwill + subject + V1?Will the vendor deliver today?

Use

  • Prediction: The load will increase in summer.
  • Promise or offer: I will send the drawing today.
  • Decision taken now: The seal is leaking - I will replace it.
  • Polite request: Will you check the panel?

Examples

Plans and predictions

  • We will start the trial tomorrow at 10 am.
  • The bearing will not last at this speed.
  • Will the spare reach before Friday?
  • I will call you after the test.

Common mistake

After will the verb never takes -s or a past form: "will comes", "will came" are wrong; write "will come". Also "will can" is wrong - use "will be able to".

Rule

Can and could express ability, permission, request and possibility. They take a bare verb: can weld, not can welds.

Uses and examples

UseExample
Ability, presentI can weld aluminium.
Ability, pastHe could weld at sixteen.
Permission, informalCan I open the panel?
Request, politeCould you send the drawing?
PossibilityThe seal could leak at high pressure.
Negative abilityI cannot lift 50 kg alone.

Examples in a workshop

One form, four jobs

  • "Can you read this drawing?" - ability
  • "Can I use the crane for ten minutes?" - permission
  • "Could you check the torque once more?" - polite request
  • "The motor could overheat in this weather." - possibility

Common mistake

"He cans weld" and "He could to weld" are both wrong. Modals never take -s and never take to (except ought to).

Rule

May is formal permission and real possibility; might is a weaker possibility.

Uses and examples

UseExample
Formal permissionMay I come in, sir?
Giving permissionYou may start the trial.
Possibility, strongThe relay may be faulty.
Possibility, weakThe relay might be faulty, but I doubt it.
WishMay you succeed in the exam.
ProhibitionVisitors may not enter the shop floor.

Examples

Choosing between them

  • "May I borrow the torque wrench?" - formal, to a senior
  • "The pump may need a new seal." - likely
  • "The pump might need a new seal." - less certain
  • "May I suggest a shorter route for the pipe?"

Common mistake

"May you please send it?" is not a request in modern English; use "Could you please send it?".

Rule

  • Must - strong obligation, order, or a logical certainty.
  • Should - advice, expectation, mild obligation.
  • Ought to - moral duty or advice; the only modal with to.

Uses and examples

UseExample
Strong obligationYou must wear goggles.
Rule or lawEvery panel must be earthed.
Logical certaintyThe tank is empty; it must have leaked.
ProhibitionYou must not open the panel live.
AdviceYou should torque the bolts in two stages.
ExpectationThe vendor should call by noon.
DutyWe ought to report the near miss.

Examples

Same situation, three strengths

  • "You must isolate the supply." - rule
  • "You should isolate the supply." - advice
  • "You ought to isolate the supply." - duty
  • "You need not isolate it for a visual check." - no obligation

Common mistake

Must not is prohibition, need not is no obligation. "You must not come" and "You need not come" are opposite instructions.

Rule

  • Shall - offers and suggestions with I/we; formal rules.
  • Will - future, promise, willingness.
  • Would - polite request, past habit, unreal condition.

Uses and examples

UseExample
OfferShall I open the window?
SuggestionShall we start the trial?
Formal ruleThe contractor shall submit the report weekly.
FutureThe line will start at 7 am.
Polite requestWould you check this reading?
Past habitHe would arrive at 7 am every day.
Unreal conditionIf I had the drawing, I would check it.

Examples

In speech and in writing

  • "Shall we begin?" - suggestion in a meeting
  • "The supervisor shall sign the job card." - a written rule
  • "I will send it today." - promise
  • "Would you mind waiting ten minutes?" - polite request

Common mistake

"I will like a coffee" is wrong; write "I would like a coffee". Would softens a wish.

h.en: 3.5 Need and the full modal table

body.en:
Need as a modal

Need behaves as a modal in the negative and the question: need not, need I? As a normal verb it takes -s and to: he needs to go.

Examples

Need and need not

  • You need not come tomorrow; the job is done.
  • The panel need not be opened for a visual check.
  • Need I sign both copies?
  • He needs to submit the report today. (normal verb)

All eleven modals by function

FunctionModalsModel sentence
Abilitycan, couldShe can weld.
Permissionmay, can, couldMay I enter?
Possibilitymay, might, couldIt may rain.
Obligationmust, should, ought toYou must report it.
Adviceshould, ought toYou should rest.
Future and offershall, will, wouldShall I help?
No obligationneed notYou need not wait.
Prohibitionmust not, may notYou must not smoke.
Past habitwould, used toHe would arrive at 7.

Common mistake

"You need not to come" is wrong: after need not the verb is bare - "you need not come".

Rule

A singular subject takes a singular verb; a plural subject takes a plural verb. In the present simple the difference is the -s: the motor runs, the motors run.

Examples

SubjectVerbSentence
one machineis / runsThe pump is running.
two machinesare / runThe pumps are running.
he, she, ithas / doesIt has a new seal.
I, we, they, youhave / doThey have new seals.

Find the subject first

Words between subject and verb do not change it

  • The box of bolts is heavy. (subject: box)
  • The boxes of bolts are heavy. (subject: boxes)
  • The reading on both meters was the same.
  • The fitters in the second shift work on line 3.

Common mistake

Matching the verb to the nearest noun instead of the subject: "The list of items are ready" is wrong; write "The list of items is ready".

h.en: 4.2 And, or, and words that do not count

body.en:
Rules

PatternVerbExample
A and BpluralThe motor and the pump are new.
A or B, either ... or, neither ... nornearest subjectEither the belt or the bearings are worn.
A with B, as well as, along with, together withfirst subjectThe supervisor, along with two fitters, was present.
Each / every + singularsingularEach machine has its own meter.
Two subjects seen as one pairsingularBread and butter is his breakfast.

Examples

In sentences

  • The fitter and the helper were on site.
  • Neither the seal nor the gland was damaged.
  • Neither the seals nor the gland was damaged.
  • The manager, with his team, is visiting the plant.

Common mistake

"As well as" is not and: "The pump as well as the motor are new" should be "is new".

Collective nouns

A group noun takes a singular verb when the group acts as one unit, and a plural verb when the members act separately.

Examples

  • The team is ready for the trial. (one unit)
  • The team are arguing among themselves. (members)
  • The batch has been dispatched.
  • The staff is trained in first aid.

Uncountables and amounts

SubjectVerbExample
uncountablesingularThe water is hot.
a sum of moneysingularFifty rupees is enough.
a distance or periodsingularTen kilometres is a long walk.
a pairpluralThe scissors are blunt.

Common mistake

"The equipment are new" is wrong; equipment, information, advice and furniture are uncountable and take singular verbs.

h.en: 4.4 Indefinite subjects and there is / there are

body.en:
Rules

SubjectVerbExample
everyone, everybody, someone, nobody, each, either, neithersingularEverybody is ready.
none of + pluralsingular or pluralNone of the bolts is loose.
some / most / half of + pluralpluralMost of the fitters are trained.
some / most / half of + uncountablesingularMost of the oil has leaked.
there is + singularsingularThere is one spare left.
there are + pluralpluralThere are two spares left.

Examples

Agreement in practice

  • Nobody knows the cause yet.
  • Each of the panels has a label.
  • None of the readings is outside the limit.
  • There are three items on the checklist.

Common mistake

"Everyone are here" and "There is two spares" are wrong. Everyone is singular; two spares is plural.

h.en: 4.5 Five traps that come up in exams

body.en:
The traps

TrapRightWhy
news, mathematics, physicsThe news is good.-s but singular
police, cattle, peopleThe police are here.always plural
one of + plural nounOne of the bolts is missing.the subject is one
a number of + pluralA number of faults were found.means many
the number of + pluralThe number of faults was small.means the count
percentage or fractionTen per cent of the batch was rejected.agrees with the noun after of

Examples

Corrected sentences

  • Wrong: "The news are bad." Right: "The news is bad."
  • Wrong: "One of the pumps are leaking." Right: "One of the pumps is leaking."
  • Wrong: "A number of men was present." Right: "A number of men were present."
  • Wrong: "Twenty per cent of the oil have leaked." Right: "Twenty per cent of the oil has leaked."

Common mistake

Reading "one of the pumps" and matching are to pumps. The subject is one.

Rule

SV is the shortest complete sentence: a subject and an intransitive verb. Nothing else is needed.

Examples

SubjectVerbFull sentence
The motorfailedThe motor failed.
The linestoppedThe line stopped.
The pumpleakedThe pump leaked.
The bellrangThe bell rang.
The operatorleftThe operator left.

Longer SV sentences

Still SV, with extra information

  • The motor failed suddenly. (adverb added)
  • The line stopped at ten. (time added)
  • The pump leaked badly. (adverb added)
  • The old motor on line 2 failed. (subject expanded)

Common mistake

Adding an object to an intransitive verb: "The motor failed the test" changes the meaning; if you name what failed, you need a transitive verb (damaged, stopped, broke).

Rule

SVO uses a transitive verb, and the object answers what? or whom? after the verb.

Examples

SubjectVerbObjectSentence
The fitterreplacedthe beltThe fitter replaced the belt.
The operatorcheckedthe oilThe operator checked the oil.
Wetestedthe relayWe tested the relay.
The companyorderedtwo pumpsThe company ordered two pumps.
Shesignedthe job cardShe signed the job card.

Find the object

Question test

  • "The helper cleaned the filter." - cleaned what? the filter → SVO
  • "The helper cleaned carefully." - cleaned how? → SV (A), no object
  • "We tested the relay at 4 pm." - tested what? the relay → SVO

Common mistake

Putting the object in the wrong place: "Replaced the fitter the belt" is wrong; the order is subject, verb, object.

Rule

SVA needs an adverbial - a word or phrase saying where, when or how - because without it the sentence is incomplete.

Examples

SubjectVerbAdverbialSentence
The pumprunssmoothlyThe pump runs smoothly.
Helivesin SuratHe lives in Surat.
The linestartsat 7 amThe line starts at 7 am.
The toolsareon the benchThe tools are on the bench.
The meetingendedat noonThe meeting ended at noon.

How to test for SVA

Remove the adverbial and see what happens

  • "He lives." - incomplete, so the adverbial is necessary → SVA
  • "The pump runs." - complete, so smoothly is optional → SV
  • "The tools are on the bench." - are needs a place → SVA
  • "The line starts at 7 am." - when is part of the meaning → SVA

Common mistake

Calling the adverbial an object. "He lives in Surat" has no object; in Surat answers where, not what.

Rule

SVC uses a linking verb (be, become, seem, look, feel, smell, taste) and a complement that describes the subject. The complement is never an object: it refers to the subject, not to something new.

Examples

SubjectVerbComplementSentence
The panelishotThe panel is hot.
The fitterbecamea supervisorThe fitter became a supervisor.
The bearinglookswornThe bearing looks worn.
The coolantsmellsburntThe coolant smells burnt.
The drawingseemsincorrectThe drawing seems incorrect.

Object or complement?

Swap test: if the two words can be swapped, it is a complement

  • "The panel is hot." → "Hot is the panel" still makes sense → complement, SVC.
  • "The fitter replaced the belt." → "The belt replaced the fitter" does not → object, SVO.
  • "He became an engineer." → "An engineer became he" works → SVC.
  • "He checked the relay." → no swap → SVO.

Common mistake

"The motor is run" (passive) is not SVC; SVC needs a describing complement: "The motor is noisy".

Four questions

QuestionAnswerPattern
Is the sentence complete after the verb?yesSV
Does what? or whom? give the rest?yesSVO
Does the rest answer where, when or how?yesSVA
Does the rest describe the subject, after be / become / seem?yesSVC

Worked examples: six sentences, sorted

SentencePatternWhy
The compressor started.SVcomplete after the verb
The operator closed the valve.SVOclosed what?
The valve is closed.SVCclosed describes the valve
The gauge reads 4 bar.SVOreads what?
The gauge is on the panel.SVAwhere
The gauge looks faulty.SVCdescribes the gauge

Beyond the syllabus

Two more patterns appear in longer sentences: SVOO (The store gave the fitter a new seal) and SVOC (The inspector found the panel hot). The syllabus examines SV, SVO, SVA and SVC.

Common mistake

Deciding by the last word instead of the question the rest answers. Always ask what? before you call something an object.

h.en: Practice 1. Name the parts of speech of the underlined words: The (a) fitter quickly (b) replaced the brass (c) valve and (d) smiled.

body.en:
(a) fitter - noun (common noun, doeser of the action).

(b) quickly - adverb of manner, describing replaced.

(c) brass - adjective (material adjective describing valve; it can also be a noun). (d) and - conjunction, joining two verb phrases.

The sentence uses four classes in nine words; label a word by the work it does in that sentence, not by a fixed label.

h.en: Practice 2. Rewrite these sentences with the correct present simple form: (a) The pump run daily. (b) He do not check the oil. (c) Does they test the relay?

body.en:
(a) The pump runs daily. - the subject is singular, so the verb takes -s.

(b) He does not check the oil. - with he, she, it use does, and the main verb stays in V1.

(c) Do they test the relay? - with they use do, and again the main verb stays in V1.

h.en: Practice 3. Fill in the correct tense: (a) The line ___ (stop) at 10:15 am yesterday. (b) I ___ (check) the panel when the alarm rang. (c) She ___ (work) here since 2022. (d) We ___ (finish) the job, so the line can start.

body.en:
(a) stopped - past simple, because yesterday is a finished time.

(b) was checking - past continuous, an action in progress when a shorter action happened.

(c) has been working - present perfect continuous with since, for an action that began in the past and is still going on; has worked is also accepted.

(d) have finished - present perfect, because the result matters now: the line can start.

h.en: Practice 4. Correct these sentences: (a) I have seen him yesterday. (b) He did not checked the torque. (c) They are knowing the answer.

body.en:
(a) I saw him yesterday. - yesterday is a finished time, so the past simple is used, not the present perfect.

(b) He did not check the torque. - after did not the verb stays in V1.

(c) They know the answer. - know is a stative verb, so it takes the simple present, not the continuous.

h.en: Practice 5. Use the correct modal: (a) ___ you please send the drawing? (polite request) (b) You ___ wear goggles in the shop. (strong obligation) (c) You ___ come tomorrow; the job is done. (no obligation) (d) The relay ___ be faulty, but I am not sure. (weak possibility)

body.en:
(a) Could you please send the drawing? - could is the modal used for a polite request.

(b) You must wear goggles in the shop. - must marks a rule and a strong obligation.

(c) You need not come tomorrow. - need not means there is no obligation; must not would mean prohibition, which is a different instruction.

(d) The relay might be faulty. - might expresses a weaker possibility than may.

h.en: Practice 6. Explain the difference between must not and need not with one example each.

body.en:
Must not forbids an action: "You must not open the panel while the supply is on." It is a rule with a safety reason.

Need not removes an obligation: "You need not open the panel for a visual check." The action is allowed, simply not necessary.

The two are opposites in practice: one stops you, the other lets you off.

h.en: Practice 7. Correct the subject-verb agreement: (a) The box of bolts are heavy. (b) One of the pumps are leaking. (c) Neither the seal nor the gland were damaged. (d) The news are bad.

body.en:
(a) The box of bolts is heavy. - the subject is box; of bolts only describes it.

(b) One of the pumps is leaking. - the subject is one, not pumps.

(c) Neither the seal nor the gland was damaged. - with neither ... nor the verb agrees with the nearer subject, which is singular here.

(d) The news is bad. - news ends in -s but is singular.

h.en: Practice 8. Give two rules of subject-verb agreement with one example each.

body.en:
A singular subject takes a singular verb and a plural subject a plural verb: "The motor runs" and "The motors run".

Words placed between the subject and the verb do not change the verb: "The list of items is ready", where the subject is list.

Two subjects joined by and take a plural verb: "The motor and the pump are new", while along with and as well as do not: "The supervisor, along with two fitters, was present".

h.en: Practice 9. Identify the pattern of each sentence: (a) The compressor started. (b) The operator closed the valve. (c) The valve is closed. (d) The gauge is on the panel.

body.en:
(a) SV - the sentence is complete after the intransitive verb started.

(b) SVO - closed what? the valve; the object is a different thing from the subject.

(c) SVC - closed describes the valve, and the two can be swapped in meaning, so it is a complement.

(d) SVA - on the panel answers where, and without it the gauge is is incomplete.

h.en: Practice 10. Write one sentence for each pattern SV, SVO, SVA and SVC about a workshop.

body.en:
SV: The drill stopped. - the sentence is complete after the intransitive verb, so nothing else is needed.

SVO: The apprentice cleaned the filter. - cleaned what? the filter, which is the object.

SVA: The compressor is in the corner. - in the corner answers where, and it cannot be left out.

SVC: The bearing feels rough. - rough describes the bearing after the linking verb feels, so it is a complement. Keep each sentence short in the exam, then name the pattern from the question that the rest of the sentence answers.

h.en: Practice 11. Change these into the tense asked for: (a) He checks the oil. (past continuous) (b) They replaced the belt. (present perfect) (c) The line stops at 10. (past simple) (d) I write the report. (future simple)

body.en:
(a) He was checking the oil.

(b) They have replaced the belt.

(c) The line stopped at 10.

(d) I will write the report. Notice that only the auxiliary and the tense-carrying verb form change; the subject, the object and the rest of the sentence stay exactly as they are.

Check every answer the same way: name the tense of the original, name the tense asked for, then change only what that tense needs.

h.en: Practice 12. Explain the difference between the present perfect and the past simple, with one example each.

body.en:
The past simple reports a finished action at a finished time: "We replaced the belt yesterday." The time is named or understood.

The present perfect reports a finished action whose result matters now, with no time named: "We have replaced the belt, so the line can start."

So "I have seen him yesterday" is wrong - the moment you name yesterday, the past simple is needed.

h.en: Practice 13. Correct these sentences and name the error: (a) He works good. (b) Myself Raj. (c) Discuss about the problem. (d) Although it was hot, but we finished.

body.en:
(a) He works well. - an adverb is needed, not the adjective good.

(b) I am Raj. - myself is reflexive and cannot replace the subject pronoun.

(c) Discuss the problem. - discuss is transitive and takes no preposition.

(d) Although it was hot, we finished. - one conjunction per link; although and but together is a double conjunction.

h.en: Practice 14. Give one example each of a preposition of place, time and agent.

body.en:
Place: "The tools are on the bench."

Time: "The line starts at 7 am."

Agent: "The joint was welded by Ashok." The agent preposition names who did the action, which is why passive sentences use by.

Keep the three questions separate in the exam: where gives a preposition of place, when a preposition of time, and by whom the agent.

h.en: Practice 15. Join each pair with a suitable conjunction: (a) The belt was loose. The line vibrated. (b) The load was high. The motor stayed cool.

body.en:
(a) Because the belt was loose, the line vibrated. - subordinating conjunction for cause.

(b) Although the load was high, the motor stayed cool. - subordinating conjunction for contrast.

(a) can also be joined with so in the other order: "The belt was loose, so the line vibrated." Both are correct; the choice changes which half is the main clause.

a.en: V1 / V1+s - he runs
am/is/are + V-ing - he is running
have/has + V3 - he has run
have/has been + V-ing - he has been running
V2 - he ran
was/were + V-ing - he was running
had + V3 - he had run
will + V1 - he will run
The motor failed.
The fitter replaced the belt.
The pump runs smoothly.
The panel is hot.

q.en: Name the eight parts of speech.

a.en: Noun, verb, pronoun, adjective, adverb, preposition, conjunction and interjection.

q.en: What is the difference between a common noun and a proper noun? Give an example.

a.en: A common noun names any member of a class (city, engineer) and takes no capital; a proper noun names one particular one (Surat, Ashok) and always takes a capital.

q.en: Give three uncountable nouns used in a workshop.

a.en: Water, oil and equipment - they have no plural form, so we say "two pieces of equipment".

q.en: What is the difference between an adjective and an adverb?

a.en: An adjective describes a noun (a hot motor); an adverb describes a verb, adjective or another adverb (the motor runs smoothly).

q.en: Give the three degrees of comparison of "good".

a.en: Good, better, best - and never "more better".

q.en: State the rule for the present simple with he, she and it.

a.en: The verb takes -s: he runs, she checks, it leaks.

q.en: When do we use the present perfect?

a.en: For a finished action with a present result or an experience with no time mentioned: "I have finished the job, so the line can start."

q.en: What is the difference between past simple and past perfect?

a.en: Past simple reports one past action ("the belt broke"); past perfect reports the earlier of two past actions ("the belt had broken before I arrived").

q.en: List the modal auxiliaries in your syllabus.

a.en: Can, could, may, might, must, shall, will, should, would, ought to and need.

q.en: What is the difference between must not and need not?

a.en: Must not is prohibition ("you must not open the panel live"); need not means no obligation ("you need not come tomorrow").

q.en: Give one sentence each with can, could and may.

a.en: Ability: "I can weld aluminium." Polite request: "Could you send the drawing?" Formal permission: "May I enter the shop floor?"

q.en: State two rules of subject-verb agreement with examples.

a.en: A singular subject takes a singular verb (the motor runs) and a plural subject a plural verb (the motors run); and two subjects joined by and take a plural verb (the motor and the pump are new).

q.en: Which verb agrees with "one of the pumps"?

a.en: A singular verb, because the subject is one: "one of the pumps is leaking".

q.en: Name the four basic sentence patterns with one example each.

a.en: SV - the motor failed; SVO - the fitter replaced the belt; SVA - the pump runs smoothly; SVC - the panel is hot.

q.en: How do you tell an object from a complement?

a.en: An object answers what or whom and is a different thing from the subject; a complement describes the subject and can be swapped with it in meaning - "the panel is hot" / "hot is the panel".

q.en: What is a transitive verb?

a.en: A verb that needs an object to complete its meaning, such as replace, check or measure: "replace the belt".
